newsitem.title: USA: U.S. imposes charges on China textile quotas.
newsitem.headline: U.S. imposes charges on China textile quotas.

text.p: Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky announced Friday punitive charges against China's 1996 textile and apparel quotas, citing transshipments of Chinese textiles in violation of a 1994 trade agreement.

The action -- which will cost China approximately $19 million -- is the first time the United States has imposed so-called "triple" charges, which are permitted in cases of repeated violations of the 1994 bilateral textiles agreement.
The new charges bring to $80 million the charges against China under the agreement, Barshefsky said in a statement.
"These charges against China's quota should be seen as part of ongoing efforts to ensure compliance with this agreement," Barshefsky said.
A probe by the U.S. Customs Service showed China worked aggessively to circumvent the agreement, the statement said.

Cotton shorts and trousers produced in China entered the United States as products of Mongolia; sewing thread, wool coats and other goods entered as products of Hong Kong; apparel products came in as products of Fiji; and jogging suits entered as products of Turkey, the statement said.

The categories of Chinese products where charges will be made include sewing thread, women's cotton coats, men's cotton knit shirts, women's cotton knit shirts, men's cotton trousers, women's cotton trousers, pyjamas, dishtowels, shoptowels, men's wool jackets, women's man-made fiber blouses, and silk blend and non-cotton vegetable fiber woven shirts and blouses.
American Textile Manufacturers Institute President James Fitzgibbons said he welcomed the action, which he said would help U.S. textile producers compete against illegal imports.
